evidence: Cic. Ac. 1.1: dē viā fessus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The standard classical word, in prose and in verse (Lewis & Short: classical, especially frequent in the poets).

terms.register: vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī et poētārum: Plaut., Hor., Juv.; nōn apud Cic. aut Caes.
evidence: Plaut. Amph. 329: Lassus sum hercle, nāvī ut vectus hūc sum
terms.comment: The everyday word of comedy and of the poets, the source of Italian lasso and French las. Lewis & Short notes that it is not in Cicero or Caesar, who say fessus and dēfessus. Plautus and Terence, for their part, say lassus (twelve times) and dēfessus (thirteen) and happen not to have fessus: that shows the register of comedy, not that fessus is rare or wrong.
Wearied by something; stronger than fessus, and rare before Augustus (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: adjective (participle of dēfetīscor), often with the ablative of a gerund: dēfessus ambulandō
terms.comment: The word of the comedies and of Cicero for being tired out by doing something. Classical and frequent as a participle (Lewis & Short s.v. dēfetīscor).

phrases.english: Are you tired? Said to a boy.
Are you tired? Said to a girl.

phrases.latin: Lassus sum hercle, nāvī ut vectus hūc sum: etiam nunc nauseō.
phrases.english: I’m worn out, by Hercules, after coming here by ship: I still feel seasick.

phrases.latin: ille opere forīs faciendō lassus noctū ad mē advenit
phrases.english: he comes home to me at night tired from working out of doors

phrases.latin: Nōn sum fessus! — Quid ergō ōscitās?
phrases.english: I’m not tired! — Then why are you yawning?
